lessons.title: What ColabFold does
lessons.summary: AlphaFold2 structure prediction, packaged to run from one command.

blocks.text:
ColabFold predicts a protein's 3D structure from its sequence. It runs AlphaFold2, DeepMind's structure prediction network, but replaces AlphaFold2's slow database search with a fast MMseqs2 search on the ColabFold server. A prediction that took hours with the original AlphaFold2 takes minutes.

In design work you use it as a check: if a designed sequence folds, in silico, into the structure you designed it for, with high confidence, it's worth ordering.

A run has three stages:

1. MSA: find related sequences (a multiple sequence alignment). Evolution tells the network which residues touch. This step needs the internet, to reach the ColabFold server.

2. Prediction: 5 AlphaFold2 models each predict the structure, refining it over several recycles. This is the part that needs a GPU.

3. Ranking: the models are ranked by confidence, and the best is called rank_001.

command.name: colabfold_batch
command.what: INPUT is a FASTA file (one query per record) or a folder of FASTA files. RESULTS is a folder for the output; it's created if needed. Available after `module load colabfold`.

try.text: Load ColabFold and read its help.

quiz.q: Which stage of a ColabFold run needs the GPU?
quiz.why: The neural network predictions run on the GPU. The MSA search runs on the ColabFold server.

lessons.title: Running it: GPU, memory and options
lessons.summary: Get a GPU, run a fold, and the options that change speed and quality.

blocks.text: ColabFold needs a GPU, so run it inside a Slurm job: interactively with srun for one quick fold, or with sbatch for anything bigger. Memory grows with sequence length; 32G covers most single chains, and big complexes may need 48G, the most one student can hold.

example.cmd:
srun --gres=gpu:1 --mem=32G --pty bash
module load colabfold
colabfold_batch binder_01.fasta binder_01_af
exit
example.note: Get a GPU, load the software, fold, give the GPU back. Modules don't carry into a new job, so load inside it.

flags: How many of the 5 AlphaFold2 models to run (default 5). 1 is 5× faster, for quick tests
Refinement passes per model (default 3; more for complexes). More can help hard targets
Skip the MSA search. Fast, and common for de novo designs, which have no relatives
Also use known structures from the PDB as hints
Clean up clashes in the top models with a short force-field minimization
With --amber, relax only the top N

blocks.tip: Test with `--num-models 1 --num-recycle 1` first. If that runs cleanly, run the full prediction in a batch job.

quiz.q: You're checking 50 de novo designs quickly. Which options make sense for a first pass?
quiz.why: One model and no MSA search is much faster, and de novo designs have no natural relatives for an MSA to find anyway.

lessons.title: Reading the results: ranks and confidence
lessons.summary: Which file is the best model, and how much to trust it.

blocks.text: For each query, the results folder holds 5 PDB files named by rank, a scores JSON for each, plots (coverage, PAE, pLDDT), and `log.txt` with the summary. The best model's file contains `rank_001`.

example.note: rank_001 is the most confident model. model_3 says which of the 5 networks made it. unrelaxed means no Amber clean-up.

flags: Per-residue confidence, 0–100. Above 90 very high, 70–90 good, 50–70 low, below 50 likely disordered
Confidence in the overall fold, 0–1. Above 0.5 suggests the fold is roughly right
For complexes: confidence in how the chains sit together. Above about 0.8 is strong; below 0.6 is doubtful
Expected position error between pairs of residues, in Å. Low PAE between binder and target means a confident interface

try.text: Pull the rank_001 line out of the log to see its pLDDT.

quiz.q: A designed binder with its target gets pLDDT 91 but ipTM 0.42. What does that suggest?
options: Both chains fold well, but the predicted binding is unreliable
quiz.why: High pLDDT means each chain's structure is confident. Low ipTM means the network isn't confident about how they bind.

lessons.title: Complexes, folders and batch jobs
lessons.summary: Fold a binder with its target, fold many designs at once, and run it all as a job.

blocks.text: To predict a complex, put the chains in one FASTA record separated by a colon. ColabFold then uses the multimer model and reports ipTM.

example.note: Binder first, a colon, then the target.

blocks.text: Give a folder instead of a file and ColabFold folds every .fasta in it, one after another, loading the model only once. It skips queries that already have a `.done.txt` file, so a run that stopped can simply be restarted.

example.out:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=fold
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --time=03:00:00
#SBATCH --output=fold-%j.out

module load colabfold
colabfold_batch designs/ designs_af/
example.note: A batch job for a folder of designs. If it runs out of memory (State OUT_OF_MEMORY), raise --mem; if it times out, rerun it: finished queries are skipped.

quiz.q: How do you write a two-chain complex for ColabFold?
options: Two records in one FASTA file
Both sequences in one record, joined by :
quiz.why: A colon inside one record tells ColabFold the chains belong to one complex. Separate records are folded separately.
